changes.what: Replaced the textbook Coase-theorem sentence (1960, transaction costs, negotiation, 'regardless of which party') with the source's railroad-sparks property-rights account: undefined rights mean squabbling and nothing done; the party with defined responsibility finds the least costly fix [V]. Added the source's guidance on when permits vs charges fit (few dozen/hundred interested traders vs millions of small emitters).
Coase connection entry: dropped 'transaction costs'; now externalities and property rights via the railroad-sparks illustration.

Lemons passage: replaced 'sellers of good cars are driven out by adverse selection' with the source's account: sellers know more and may hide problems, prices still reflect reputation; higher-quality sellers 'may be reluctant to participate', buyers unwilling to pay more, markets 'may become extremely thin' [V]. 'Adverse selection' now appears only in the insurance and wage-cut contexts, as in the source.

Ch 16.2: premiums priced on the probability of events among a pool [V]; adverse events come from characteristics and choices plus 'the good or bad luck of what actually happens' [V]; risk groups charged 'according to its expected losses' = 'actuarially fair' [V].
Ch 17.2: bond interest-rate risk as opportunity cost; present discounted value defined as what you would need now to equal a future amount, requiring an interest rate.

New 'Appendix C: Present discounted value' section: PDV definition [V], interest rate as opportunity cost of capital plus risk premium [V], expected profits a best guess [V], uses outside finance, 'indispensable tool' whenever costs and benefits stretch into the future [V].

Ch 6.3 self-control detail: pack-not-carton, fridge locks, overpaying taxes to force saving, 'we protect ourselves from our worst temptations but pay a price to do so' [V]; nudges and automatic retirement enrolment. (The source has no present bias, time preference or discounting material in Ch 6.3.)

Ch 5.3 cost pass-through: 'Elasticity also reveals whether firms can pass higher costs that they incur on to consumers' [V]; inelastic demand lets firms pass increases on, elastic demand cuts quantity instead.
Ch 5.3 tax incidence: 'Typically, the tax incidence, or burden, falls both on the consumers and producers of the taxed good' [V] before the existing more-inelastic-side rule.
Ch 2.1 marginal analysis: people often look at total costs and total benefits when the optimal choice needs a comparison of how they change [V].

Ch 11.4 regulatory capture: source's definition [V] and airline-board mechanism (appointees, lobbyists, information, jobs for departing board members), so distillations can cite what capture looks like.

Ch 13.3 Ostrom: she challenged the regulation-or-property-rights-only view; farmers could communicate and cooperate; resources are better managed without external influence when beneficiaries are close by [BT]. Supports the distillation fixes that drop invented design principles.
Ch 18 intro: Olson launched the modern study of public economy [BT], 'sometimes referred to as public choice, a subtopic of microeconomics' [V].
